SCHOOL GARDEN · GARDEN FRIENDS

Garden Animals & Friends

Age 2 YearsSubject Nature & TalkClass School GardenDuration 3–5 minutes

A bird in the hedge, a worm after the rain, an owl you might only hear — meet the animals that live around gardens and the great outdoors, one big picture at a time.

Nothing to prepare and nothing to read to your toddler. You say the name, they point or hop — a moment on a card counts, and the real outdoors can wait for your next walk.

TOGETHER · WHERE MIGHT WE SEE IT?

Where might we see it?

Some of these friends live in gardens, some just visit, and some live in the wider outdoors — here is where to look, gently and from a distance.

  • Bird

    “Hedges, parks and balconies — you will hear one before you see it.”

  • Squirrel

    “Up in the trees of any leafy park, tail twitching.”

  • Duck

    “On ponds and canals, paddling along in a little line.”

  • Rabbit

    “At the edges of meadows and gardens, early in the morning.”

  • Frog

    “Near ponds, puddles and damp grass, especially after rain.”

  • Worm

    “In the soil and under flowerpots after it rains — look, then leave them be.”

  • Hedgehog

    “In hedges and leaf piles after dark, if you are lucky.”

  • Bat

    “Flitting through the evening sky just after sunset.”

  • Owl

    “High in old trees at night — usually a whooo long before a look.”

SOLVE THE SHEETS — ON PAPER OR ON SCREEN

Solve the garden animal cards together.

The twenty garden animal cards print two to a page, straight from your browser. Printed, cut and named, they are the collection’s real worksheets — and on screen, every card page can be drawn on directly.

  1. 01

    Print the cards

    Open the printable cards and print all twenty, two to a page. Cut them out together, naming each garden animal as it is cut.

  2. 02

    Name and greet

    Hold up a card and greet the friend — “hello, owl!”. Naming warmly is how animal words stick at two.

  3. 03

    Move like them

    Hop like a frog, flap like a bird, twitch like a squirrel. Guessing from a movement is the game the whole room can play.

  4. 04

    Find them outside

    Carry two or three cards on the next walk and find their real twins. We look, we talk, and the animals stay where they live.

Open the printable sheets ↗Draw on the cards on screen ↗

Every card page has a Write & Color layer: your child can draw right on the card with a finger, a stylus or the mouse, then save the finished work. Nothing is uploaded anywhere.

TAKE IT OFF SCREEN

A look-don’t-touch nature hunt.

Take the names outside — or to a window, a book or a video if the outdoors is far away. Wild animals are looked at, never touched, chased or fed.

Try one today

  • Spot a bird from the window and say its name together.
  • Watch a squirrel’s tail twitch in the park.
  • After rain, look for a worm on the path — look with your eyes, then walk on by.
  • At dusk, look up and search for bats — pointing and whispering is plenty.
  • Hop like a frog and wiggle like a worm yourselves — the safest animals to touch are you two.

Never feed wild animals, never touch or pick up an unknown animal, and never follow one for a closer look. A grown-up stays close the whole time — one spotted friend is a complete hunt.

A NOTE FROM THE PRINCIPAL

For the grown-ups.

Your toddler does not need every animal name to stick. Saying words while they look and hop is the whole lesson — the vocabulary rides along, and no garden is required. Some of these friends live in gardens, some only visit, and some live in the wider outdoors — all of that is fine to wonder about together.

TIPS FOR PARENTS

Tips for Parents

Follow your toddler’s favourites. If the frog gets five rounds in a row, the frog gets five rounds in a row — repetition is how little ones learn.

Sounds and movement before facts. Hopping, wiggling and quacking teach the names better than any explanation, so be as silly as your toddler needs you to be.

Keep it honest and gentle: some of these animals live in gardens, some just visit and some stay far outdoors — and all of them stay wild. Looking is the game; touching, feeding and chasing are not part of it.

Age ranges are a guide. Go at your child’s pace.

    Bird — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    This lesson turns the bird card into your toddler’s first watching game: name the bird, notice it move, then keep still together and let a real one arrive on its own.

    What is this?

    A bird is an animal with feathers and wings that flies and sings. Birds visit gardens, hedges and windowsills every morning, looking for seeds and crumbs.

    What does it mean?

    Birds give a two-year-old the day’s first magic trick: something appears, moves and disappears on its own schedule. Learning to watch without touching is the deepest thing the card teaches.

    What does the child need to know?

    The one big idea: birds come to the still and quiet. Running feet send them away. We look at birds, we talk softly to them, and our hands stay down.

    Why this matters

    Watching a bird is a toddler’s first lesson in patience with a payoff — the stiller they sit, the longer the bird stays. That cause and effect is learned in the body, no words needed.

    What it teaches

    Attention and stillness (a real skill at two), first nature vocabulary, cause-and-effect noticing, pointing and naming, and the gentle beginnings of caring about living things.

    Words to learn

    birdfeatherswingsseedsquietfly

    Say this to your child

    “"Here is the bird! Birds have wings and they fly. When we get quiet like this — ssh — and watch out the window, a bird might come and say hello. Birds are watch-friends — chasing only sends them away. Quiet feet find birds."”

    Step by step

    1. Show the card and say the word bird slowly, twice — then make a little tweet together so the word arrives with a sound.
    2. Ask your toddler to find the bird’s beak and its wing on the card with one finger — pointing is how twos study a picture.
    3. Carry the card to a window and whisper: "maybe a bird is outside right now." Looking quietly is the game, and the whisper sets its mood.
    4. Sprinkle a few seeds on a sill or step, stand back, and count the seconds of stillness out loud — even ten quiet ones deserve applause.
    5. End with the rule, warm and short: birds are our look-at friends — hands down, feet still, and they come close all by themselves.

    Look closer at the picture

    Find the bird on the card with one fingertip. Say bird together, then make a little tweet. Ask where the beak is and where the wing is — pointing is a two-year-old’s way of studying a picture.

    Ask your child

    "What does the bird say?" "Can you point to the wing?" "Where did the bird go?" "Were your quiet feet still?" — questions a two-year-old can answer with a sound, a point or a giggle.

    What your child can say or do

    "Tweet tweet!" "Bird gone!" Your toddler may press their nose to the window, freeze dramatically still for three whole seconds, or point at pigeons, crows and ducks on every walk afterwards, calling each one bird.

    Out in the real world

    Birds are the most reliable wildlife in any street: on the sill, in the hedge, strutting across the car park at the shop. Each sighting is a rerun of the lesson — point, whisper, watch, wave goodbye.

    Try it together

    Seed sprinkle and freeze: shake a tiny cup of seeds onto a step, then play freeze together — crouch, hold hands tight, breathe loudly enough to hear, and wait. Whoever stays frozen longest wins, and the prize is usually a bird.

    Understanding check

    Watch what happens at the next window: if your toddler drops to a whisper and points instead of banging on the glass, the lesson has landed — stillness was the whole point.

    Parent tips

    Keep one card by the window permanently. Two minutes is a full sitting at this age; stop while the pointing is still happy. Name the big obvious kinds as they come — black bird, big beak — precision can wait years.

    Staying safe

    Windows and doors stay shut while you watch together, and the sill stays for seeds, not elbows. If you feed birds, do it outside where they stay wild — and wash little hands after touching seed.

    This lesson pairs with the Bird flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Garden Friends (School Garden).

    Frog — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    This lesson gets the wiggles out and the word in: your toddler becomes the frog, leaps across a cushion pond, and learns that real frogs live by water where grown-up eyes do the finding.

    What is this?

    A frog is a small green or brown animal with long back legs that hops high and swims well. Frogs live near ponds and puddles and catch bugs with a quick flick of the tongue.

    What does it mean?

    The frog is the movement card of the set — jumping is what a two-year-old’s legs have been waiting to do. Naming the animal while being the animal is how the word sinks all the way in.

    What does the child need to know?

    Two things to know: frogs jump and say ribbit, and real frogs live down by the water where we go with a grown-up. We watch them from the bank; their skin stays untouched.

    Why this matters

    Big jumps build balance, leg strength and landing control — genuine physical milestones dressed as a game. And the pond rule plants early respect: some animals are for looking, and that is not a loss, it is the friendship.

    What it teaches

    Gross motor power (crouch, launch, land), listening and responding ("jump!... freeze!"), animal vocabulary, and early self-control — the same legs that leap must also stop.

    Words to learn

    frogjumppondribbitlily padhop

    Say this to your child

    “"Can you be a frog? Crouch down low... and JUMP! Ribbit! Frogs have long strong legs and they live near the pond. When we see a real frog, we stand still and watch it — our hands stay in our pockets and our eyes do the finding."”

    Step by step

    1. Show the card, say frog, and crouch down low yourself — your toddler will copy your shape before they copy your word.
    2. Do one big jump together and land with a plop — then say ribbit! Linking word, jump and sound is the whole lesson in three seconds.
    3. Spread cushions across the floor — your lily pads — and hop between them, whispering ribbit on every landing to keep it playful, not wild.
    4. Tell the pond story simply: real frogs sit by the water, and we look at them from the bank with a grown-up, hands tucked away.
    5. Finish by crouching very small and still — a hiding frog — then one last huge jump to end on a laugh.

    Look closer at the picture

    Who is on the card? Say frog out loud, then crouch and do one big frog jump right there. Ask where the frog’s eyes are, and finish with a ribbit — the picture, the jump and the sound make the whole introduction.

    Ask your child

    "Where does the frog live?" "Can you jump like the frog?" "What does the frog say?" "Do we touch the froggy at the pond, or only look?" — each one lands with a jump, a sound or a solemn little head-shake.

    What your child can say or do

    "Ribbit!" "Froggy jump!" Expect cushion-leaping for days, frogs spotted in puddles that are actually shadows, and the proud announcement "frog see it!" after any walk near water.

    Out in the real world

    Frogs turn up after rain, at pond edges, even in window wells — and every spot-the-frog moment reruns the rule for free. Between sightings, puddles and bath time keep the leaping going.

    Try it together

    Lily-pad musical frogs: scatter cushions, play a hum or a song, and leap pad to pad. When the music stops, every frog crouches tiny and still. Freeze plus jump is the toddler combination hit.

    Understanding check

    Ask for the sound and the move at a random moment tomorrow: if a crouch-jump-ribbit arrives unprompted, the word and the animal are glued together — lesson complete.

    Parent tips

    Soft landing spots only — rugs and cushions, never hard floors. Join every jump yourself; your leap is worth ten explanations. If a real frog is found, admire it, then steer away before small hands get ideas.

    Staying safe

    Leaping needs clear floor — slide the coffee table out of the flight path first. By real water, one grown-up holds one small hand at all times, and frogs are never picked up; their damp skin is delicate and ours is far too warm.

    This lesson pairs with the Frog flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Garden Friends (School Garden).

    Squirrel — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    This lesson borrows the squirrel’s own game — dash, stop, look — and hands it to your toddler: scurry like a squirrel at home, then freeze and spot the real one from the path.

    What is this?

    A squirrel is a small furry animal with a big bushy tail that climbs trees and buries nuts to eat later. Squirrels dash along fences and branches all day long.

    What does it mean?

    Squirrels are the only wild animal a toddler sees almost daily, doing something a toddler loves: hurrying. Naming the dash and the tail gives your child a script for every park visit from now on.

    What does the child need to know?

    The squirrel game has two moves: scurry fast, then freeze and look around — that is exactly how real squirrels behave. And the watching rule holds: we look at squirrels; our hands stay low.

    Why this matters

    Freeze-and-watch is an attention exercise disguised as play, and spotting a squirrel in a tree is your toddler’s first genuine search-and-find. Owning an animal they see every day builds the confident feeling that the world is knowable.

    What it teaches

    Visual tracking (eyes following the dash), impulse control in miniature (freeze!), climbing-and-crouching movement play, vocabulary for tails and trees, and the pride of a spot announced loudly.

    Words to learn

    squirreltailtreenutsdashclimb

    Say this to your child

    “"Look — a squirrel! See the big fluffy tail? Squirrels run up the tree, stop, and look around. Can you scurry like a squirrel? Now freeze... and watch. We look at squirrels from far away, and they put on their show for us."”

    Step by step

    1. Hold up the card and say squirrel with a big wagging arm behind you — a make-believe tail makes the new word unforgettable.
    2. Play the squirrel’s own game indoors: scurry three steps, stop, look left, look right, scurry again — narrating each move as you both do it.
    3. Hide a toy nut under one of three cups, shuffle slowly, and let your toddler find it — squirrels always remember where their food is hiding.
    4. Take the card outside to any tree and whisper the question: is a squirrel up there right now? Eyes only, quiet feet.
    5. Close with the rule, spoken with a smile: squirrels are look-at friends — we watch their tails, and our hands stay by our sides.

    Look closer at the picture

    Look for the squirrel’s tail on the card and wag an arm-tail of your own. Say squirrel twice, then ask what the tail is doing — bushy is the word you are fishing for with your toddler.

    Ask your child

    "Where is the squirrel going?" "What is its tail doing?" "Can you freeze like a squirrel?" "Did we touch the squirrel, or watch it?" — answered with a dash, a freeze and a proud point.

    What your child can say or do

    "Squirrel!" shouted at full volume in every park. Expect arm-tail wagging at dinner, nut-hiding games under cushions, and the first honest freeze when a real squirrel crosses the path — the watching rule working exactly as built.

    Out in the real world

    Squirrels live wherever trees do: the garden, the park, the churchyard, the tree outside the bakery. Every dash between branches is a rerun — point, whisper, follow with your eyes only.

    Try it together

    Three-cup nut hunt: hide a nut (or any small toy) under one cup, shuffle, and let your squirrel find it. Swap jobs — being the hider is the cleverer half of the game.

    Understanding check

    On the next walk, watch your toddler’s feet when a squirrel appears: still feet and a pointing finger mean the lesson landed — the freeze has replaced the chase.

    Parent tips

    Follow real squirrels with your eyes, never your feet — say that line on every sighting until your toddler finishes it for you. Keep the cup game tiny: three cups, one toy, big celebration.

    Staying safe

    Chasing is the danger here — a toddler dashing after a squirrel stops watching for paths and prams. Hold hands near roads, and let your fingers, not theirs, do any nut-handling; unknown nuts are not for mouths.

    This lesson pairs with the Squirrel flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Garden Friends (School Garden).

    Rabbit — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    This lesson teaches the rabbit card with the whole body: hopping across the rug, wiggling a nose, then meeting the rule that real rabbits are soft to look at and careful with.

    What is this?

    A rabbit is a soft, gentle animal with long ears and strong back legs that hops. Rabbits live in burrows underground and munch grass and leaves.

    What does it mean?

    Rabbits are usually the first animal a toddler names from books, so this card lands on friendly ground. The lesson’s real gift is gentleness: a big animal feeling practised on a small, shy creature.

    What does the child need to know?

    Rabbits hop, twitch their noses and have long listening ears. Wild rabbits are quick and shy — we watch from a step away, and even friendly-looking ones stay unpetted.

    Why this matters

    Gentle is a skill, not a mood. Practising soft hands, quiet feet and a kind voice on the rabbit card builds the exact movements your toddler will need around pets, babies and other people’s things.

    What it teaches

    Gross motor (two-foot hops), body imitation (nose twitches are surprisingly hard and wonderfully funny), gentle-touch practice on a toy, and animal vocabulary with a feeling attached.

    Words to learn

    rabbithopearssoftnosegentle

    Say this to your child

    “"A rabbit! Rabbits have long ears and they hop, hop, hop. Can you hop? Can you twitch your nose like this? When we see a real bunny, we stay quiet and soft — hands down — and watch it hop away. Gentle hands, gentle feet."”

    Step by step

    1. Show the card, say rabbit, and hop once — the word and the bounce should arrive as one event.
    2. Twitch your nose dramatically and wait: the copy may take a few tries, and the first successful twitch always earns a laugh.
    3. Hop a little rabbit trail across the room together, pausing at each stop to sniff the air like rabbits checking for danger.
    4. Hand your toddler a plush toy and practise the soft pat — one finger, slow and gentle — saying "gentle" as they do it.
    5. End with the rule in toddler words: real bunnies are watch-friends; we keep our hands to ourselves and let them hop away first.

    Look closer at the picture

    Say rabbit together, then hop once on the spot. Ask your toddler to point out the ears on the card — long ones — and finish by twitching your noses at each other like two rabbits in the rug-meadow.

    Ask your child

    "What does the bunny do?" "Can you hop two times?" "Where are its long ears?" "Do we touch the bunny or watch it?" — every answer arrives as a movement or a solemn nod, which is exactly right at two.

    What your child can say or do

    "Hop hop!" "Bunny!" Expect spontaneous nose-twitching at breakfast, rabbits spotted in every field and storybook, and a soft one-finger pat on the cat or the teddy — the gentleness practice escaping into real life.

    Out in the real world

    Rabbits appear in gardens at dusk, at petting farms, in every second picture book. Each one is a rerun: name it, admire its ears, watch from a little distance, wave goodbye.

    Try it together

    Carrot patch: cut carrot shapes from orange paper, scatter them, and let your rabbit-hop toddler gather them into a basket — hopping to each one, nose twitching, big feet and quiet landings.

    Understanding check

    Say "bunny" out of nowhere tonight: if a hop or a nose twitch comes back before the word does, the card did its work — the animal now lives in your toddler’s legs.

    Parent tips

    Practise the soft pat on toys daily; the hands learn faster than the rules do. If a real rabbit bolts away, treat it as the happy ending it is — "the bunny hopped home!" keeps watching sweet, never disappointing.

    Staying safe

    Hop on rugs, not tiles — hopping and hard floors collide. At farms, hands stay outside every hutch, and any animal touching is done to the plush toy only; real rabbits bite when startled and toddlers startle them.

    This lesson pairs with the Rabbit flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Garden Friends (School Garden).

    Hedgehog — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    This lesson turns the hedgehog card into a hiding game with a safety lesson folded inside: curl small, peek gently, and understand that some friends are loved from a distance.

    What is this?

    A hedgehog is a small animal whose back is covered in sharp spikes called spines. It snuffles around at night eating slugs and bugs, and curls into a ball when it feels unsafe.

    What does it mean?

    The hedgehog carries the set’s clearest boundary: prickly means do-not-touch. For a two-year-old, meeting that boundary in a story-shaped way — curl small, peek out — makes the rule feel wise, not cruel.

    What does the child need to know?

    Two facts and one rule: hedgehogs have spines instead of soft fur, they come out at night, and we never touch them — the spikes are for protection, and we protect them right back by keeping our hands away.

    Why this matters

    Toddlers learn some-things-are-not-for-hands from animals first, because the reason is visible — spines! A boundary with a visible reason is the easiest boundary for a two-year-old to accept and remember.

    What it teaches

    Body shaping (curling into a ball takes real control), gentle curiosity about other creatures’ bodies, the night-and-day idea, and early empathy: the hedgehog curls up because it feels safer, just like you sometimes.

    Words to learn

    hedgehogspikescurlnightsnufflegentle

    Say this to your child

    “"This is a hedgehog! Its back is full of tiny spikes — prickly, prickly! When it feels shy, it curls into a little ball, like this. Hedgehogs come out at night, and we never touch them. We look, we whisper hooray, and we let it snuffle on its way."”

    Step by step

    1. Show the card, say hedgehog, and run one fingertip very lightly along your own arm — prickly, prickly — so the spikes arrive as a feeling.
    2. Curl up on the rug into a tight ball together, then peek out with only a nose showing — the hedgehog’s own hiding trick, and toddlers adore it.
    3. Snuffle around the room like hedgehogs hunting supper — soft snuffling noises, slow wandering, one imaginary slug eaten each.
    4. Explain the night habit simply: hedgehogs wake up when we go to bed, so a garden torch from the window is how we might ever see one.
    5. Land the rule warmly: hedgehogs are prickly, so our hands stay far away — we love them by leaving them be.

    Look closer at the picture

    Find the hedgehog together and say its long name slowly — hedge-hog. Curl up small like the animal on the card, peek out with a nose, and ask what covers its back. Prickles is the answer worth waiting for.

    Ask your child

    "What does the hedgehog have on its back?" "Can you curl up small?" "When does the hedgehog wake up?" "Do our hands touch the hedgehog, or stay far away?" — answered with a curl, a whisper and a firm little head-shake.

    What your child can say or do

    "Prickly!" "Hedgehog night-night!" Expect curl-up games at bedtime that double as wind-down, hedgehogs suspected under every bush, and the rule quoted back in emergencies — including, eventually, at you: "no touch!"

    Out in the real world

    Hedgehogs visit gardens after dark, snuffling along fences; most toddlers meet them in stories first, which is fine preparation. Any night sighting from a window becomes the day’s headline.

    Try it together

    Hedgehog hide-and-peek: curl up under a light blanket, peek out with a nose, hide again — then swap and let your hedgehog find YOU curled up. Slow, dark and cosy by design.

    Understanding check

    Ask tomorrow what a hedgehog feels like: if the answer is prickly paired with pulling your hand back, both the word and the boundary have landed — the lesson is complete.

    Parent tips

    Let the curl-up game double as the calm-down trick on stormy days — a body that knows how to curl small can find calm on purpose. Never demo spines with real objects; the fingertip-on-arm pantomime carries the idea safely.

    Staying safe

    Real hedgehogs are strictly hands-off: spines scratch, and they can carry ticks and fleas. If a hedgehog calls by after dark, a shallow dish of water is the kind welcome — bread and milk make them ill, so those stay inside.

    This lesson pairs with the Hedgehog flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Garden Friends (School Garden).
