    Worm — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    This lesson makes the least glamorous card the most important one: your toddler learns the worm’s job, wiggles like one on the rug, and practises the gentlest feet in the garden.

    What is this?

    A worm is a long, thin, soft creature that lives in the soil. It eats old leaves and turns them into food for plants — the underground gardener, working all day in the dark.

    What does it mean?

    Worms teach a two-year-old that important things can be quiet and hidden. No worm, no garden — and that idea, tiny as it seems, is the first brick of every ecosystem lesson your child will ever have.

    What does the child need to know?

    Worms wiggle and live underground; rain brings them up to the path. We look with our eyes and let them be — dry hands hurt their soft skin, so they stay where the wet ground keeps them.

    Why this matters

    Watching a worm stretch and pull is mesmerising for a toddler and quietly teaches respect for small life. It is also the first time many children grasp that some animals have jobs — and the worm’s job feeds everything else.

    What it teaches

    Observation of tiny movements, new sensory words (wiggly, squishy, damp), kindness practise at its smallest and safest, and early cause-and-effect: leaves get eaten, plants get fed, garden grows.

    Words to learn

    wormwigglesoilrainsoftgarden

    Say this to your child

    “"A worm! Wiggle, wiggle! Worms live down in the dark soil and munch old leaves — they help the flowers grow. After rain they come up to say hello. We look with our eyes, our hands stay down, and the worm keeps digging."”

    Step by step

    1. Show the card, say worm, and wiggle one arm like a wavy noodle — the word should come wiggling out of your mouth too.
    2. Lie on the rug and wiggle your whole bodies along the floor together, slow and stretchy, from one cushion to another.
    3. Tell the worm’s job in two sentences: it eats old leaves underground and turns them into plant food — the garden’s own tiny helper.
    4. After the next shower, go worm-spotting on the path — crouch low, hands clasped behind backs, and watch one stretch and pull.
    5. Close with the kindness: worms are soft and their skin likes the wet earth, so we look and walk on, leaving it to its work.

    Look closer at the picture

    Say worm and wiggle an arm like a wavy noodle. Ask what the worm is doing on the card — wiggling somewhere, always — and let your toddler answer with a whole-body wiggle along the rug.

    Ask your child

    "Where does the worm live?" "Can you wiggle like a worm?" "What came before our walk — rain or sun?" "Do we touch the wormy, or watch?" — answered with a wiggle and a practised hands-behind-back.

    What your child can say or do

    "Wiggle wiggle!" "Wormy go home!" Expect floor-wiggling races, worms announced at full volume after every shower, and the proudest hands-behind-back crouch you have ever seen at a puddle’s edge.

    Out in the real world

    Worms arrive after every rain, on paths, patios and driveways. Each sighting is a rerun of the whole lesson in ten seconds: name it, crouch, watch, walk on — kindness complete.

    Try it together

    Scarf worm: take a scarf or skipping rope and wiggle it along the floor like a worm on the move — then let your toddler hold one end while you hold the other, wiggling together in time.

    Understanding check

    Watch the next rainy walk: if your toddler crouches, points and keeps both hands firmly behind their back, the watching rule and the worm both landed — no further lesson required.

    Parent tips

    Keep a mental note of damp worm corners near your home so a sighting is always a two-minute walk away. If the wiggle-game gets too silly for indoors, move it to the grass — wiggling was always an outdoor sport.

    Staying safe

    Worms are the safest animal on the card precisely because touching is off the table — their skin breathes, and dry little hands harm them. After worm-watching and any garden play, hands get washed before snacks.

    This lesson pairs with the Worm flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Garden Friends (School Garden).

    LEARNING PATH LESSON · GARDEN FRIENDS · AGES 2 YEARS

    Duck — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    This lesson takes the most-loved pond animal and gives it a body-and-voice routine: waddle, bill hands, quack — then the bank rule that keeps real ducks healthy and your toddler dry.

    What is this?

    A duck is a water bird with a flat bill and webbed feet that paddles on ponds and rivers. It dabbles tail-up in the water looking for plants and little water bugs.

    What does it mean?

    Ducks are usually the wildest animal a two-year-old gets close to, which makes them the perfect practice ground for every watching rule — close enough to be thrilling, far enough to be safe.

    What does the child need to know?

    Ducks say quack and paddle with their feet; they stay on the water and we stay on the land. Bread is off the menu — it makes ducks ill — so we bring our eyes and our quacks instead.

    Why this matters

    The pond edge is a natural boundary your toddler can see and feel: water here, bank there, ducks between. A rule with a visible line is the easiest kind for a two-year-old to keep — and quacking from the bank keeps the fun on the right side of it.

    What it teaches

    Gross motor comedy (waddling is a genuine balance challenge), sound imitation, the water-and-land idea, caring-from-a-distance behaviour, and first lessons in what different animal homes look like.

    Words to learn

    duckquackpondwaddlewaterbill

    Say this to your child

    “"Quack, quack! A duck! Ducks paddle on the water with their flat feet and dabble for their dinner. Can you waddle across the room? At the pond we stand on the bank with me and call quack — the ducks stay in their water, we stay on ours."”

    Step by step

    1. Show the card, say duck, and put your hands together like a flat bill — opening and closing it as you say quack.
    2. Waddle across the room together, heels together, elbows out — the sillier the waddle, the faster the word sticks.
    3. Float an empty story: the duck dabbles tail-up for supper, then paddles off — act the dabbling with a bottom wiggle for maximum giggles.
    4. At a real pond, stand a step back from the edge, hold hands, and quack a hello to the ducks — that is the correct amount of close.
    5. Explain the bread rule on the walk home: ducks eat their own pond food, and sharing our bread makes their tummies poorly.

    Look closer at the picture

    Say duck, make bill-hands with your fingers, and quack. Ask your toddler to find the bill on the card, then waddle one slow circuit of the room together before anyone sits back down.

    Ask your child

    "What does the duck say?" "Can you waddle to the door and back?" "Where do ducks live — the water or the grass?" "Do we feed the ducks bread, or just say hello?" — answered with waddling, quacking and a serious little no.

    What your child can say or do

    "Quack quack!" at every pond, puddle and bath. Expect bill-hands at dinner, waddle races down the hall, and ducks greeted by name from the buggy — with the bread rule quoted back at any grown-up who pulls out a sandwich.

    Out in the real world

    Ducks live on almost every pond, canal and river in town — the most reliable wild visit of all. Each one reruns the routine: waddle to the bank, hand held, quack, watch them dabble, wave goodbye.

    Try it together

    Pond crossing: lay a blue blanket as the pond, and waddle round its edge together — on the grass, never in the water — quacking at any ducks, socks or siblings found floating there.

    Understanding check

    Ask at the next pond visit who feeds the ducks: if the answer is "nobody — they eat pond food," the rule took root. A waddle on request seals the lesson.

    Parent tips

    Bring a small bag of defrosted peas or corn if you must feed — but the quack-from-the-bank game is honestly enough. Keep the waddle on grass and rugs; pavements punish falling toddlers.

    Staying safe

    Pond edges are grown-up territory: one hand stays held the whole visit, prams parked behind you. Never let a toddler dangle feet or hands in duck water, and wash hands after any pond-side visit before snacks.

    This lesson pairs with the Duck flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Garden Friends (School Garden).

    LEARNING PATH LESSON · GARDEN FRIENDS · AGES 2 YEARS

    Turtle — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    This lesson celebrates the opposite of hurry: your toddler walks as slowly as they can, tucks into a shell and discovers that slow is a kind of clever.

    What is this?

    A turtle is an animal that carries its hard shell on its back and moves very slowly. The shell is its house — when it feels unsafe, its head and legs pull inside.

    What does it mean?

    At two, everything is fast: legs, moods, days. The turtle card gives your child permission to try the other speed, and slowness turns out to be a skill they can practise and show off.

    What does the child need to know?

    Turtles carry their house everywhere and never rush. The game is to move slow... so slow — and the shell rule: when a turtle tucks in, it is asking for quiet, so we give it space.

    Why this matters

    Slow-motion control is genuinely hard for toddlers and builds exactly the body regulation they will need for waiting, listening and sitting at preschool. Practising it as turtle play feels like play, not practice.

    What it teaches

    Motor control at both extremes (very slow walking after weeks of dashing), patience in seconds-long doses, the shell-as-home idea, and pretending — the first kind of imaginative play with a rule.

    Words to learn

    turtleslowshellhousewaitwalk

    Say this to your child

    “"A turtle! Slow... so slow. The turtle carries its house on its back — hard and strong — and pulls its head in when it wants quiet. Can you walk like a turtle? Slower... slower... wonderful. The turtle is never in a hurry, and it always gets there."”

    Step by step

    1. Show the card, say turtle, and walk one exaggerated ultra-slow step — your toddler will match your pace before they match your word.
    2. Hold a slow-motion race: cross the whole room as slowly as possible; the loser is whoever speeds up, so dawdle shamelessly.
    3. Play shell: hug your own knees, tuck your head, then peek out — and let your toddler take a turn being the shell.
    4. Put a cushion on their back during a turtle walk and see if they can carry their house without tipping it — slow becomes necessary.
    5. End with the turtle fact as a lullaby-line: turtles carry their home everywhere, and they are never, ever late — turning up exactly when they turn up.

    Look closer at the picture

    Say turtle and ask where its house is — on its back, carried everywhere. Then walk one exaggerated slow-motion step so the card’s speed becomes the room’s speed. Slower... good.

    Ask your child

    "Where is the turtle’s house?" "Can you walk slow like a turtle?" "Is the turtle fast or slow?" "What does a turtle do when it feels shy?" — answered with a dawdle, a tuck and a whisper.

    What your child can say or do

    "Sooo slow!" Expect slow-motion walking demanded at bedtime, cushions balanced on backs, and the shell game played under tables. "Turtle" may become your family’s word for taking it easy — that is a gift.

    Out in the real world

    Turtles show up at ponds, in books and at the pet shop window; tortoises in warm gardens count too. Every slow sighting is a rerun — and any queue, wait or long car ride is turtle-training time.

    Try it together

    Turtle school: crawl under a table or blanket with a cushion shell, carry it around a chair, and park it back on the rug without dropping it. Slow wins, always — that is the whole syllabus.

    Understanding check

    Next time waiting is hard — a queue, a lift, dinner on the way — try "let us walk like a turtle there": if the pace drops and the mood lifts, the lesson is living in your toddler.

    Parent tips

    Grown-ups must genuinely lose the slow race now and then; nothing cements a game like beating the adult. Keep the cushion light and the shell brief — a minute of turtle is a full session at two.

    Staying safe

    Cushion shells stay light and never cover faces — no blankets over heads during shell play. Real turtles and tortoises are watched, not picked up; their beaks nip and their space is their own.

    This lesson pairs with the Turtle flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Garden Friends (School Garden).

    LEARNING PATH LESSON · GARDEN FRIENDS · AGES 2 YEARS

    Mouse — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    This lesson shrinks the whole body down to mouse-size: tiny steps, tiny squeaks, hiding behind the sofa — plus the respectful distance that keeps shy animals shy and safe.

    What is this?

    A mouse is a very small furry animal with big ears, a long thin tail and quick little feet. Mice hide in quiet corners and come out at dusk to look for crumbs and seeds.

    What does it mean?

    The mouse is the set’s lesson in smallness — everything about it is a size word your toddler can act out with their body. It is also the set’s lesson in shyness: some creatures want to stay hidden, and letting them is the kind move.

    What does the child need to know?

    Mice are tiny, quick and shy; they squeak and tiptoe. If a real one is ever spotted, we stay put and watch for a second, then tell a grown-up — we never follow it into corners or cupboards.

    Why this matters

    Tiptoeing is balance and control at its trickiest, and a toddler who can move quietly has mastered their body in a new register. The shy-animal rule also generalises beautifully: it is the same courtesy they will owe the cat, the baby and new friends.

    What it teaches

    Slow controlled movement (tiptoeing), whisper-voice practice, size vocabulary (tiny, little, small), understanding that animals have feelings about being seen, and dramatic hiding play.

    Words to learn

    mousetinysqueaktiptoehidewhiskers

    Say this to your child

    “"A little mouse! Squeak! Mice are tiny and quick, with whiskers and a long tail. They tiptoe out at night when everything is quiet. If we see one, we stay still and let it run home — shhh — a mouse likes to be hidden, and that is how we are kind to it."”

    Step by step

    1. Show the card, say mouse, and make yourself small — crouched, hands up as tiny paws — before you say another word.
    2. Squeak together, loudly once and then in a proper mouse whisper; the contrast teaches quiet better than any shushing.
    3. Tiptoe across the room on a mouse mission — fetch one crumb (a block), carry it back under the table, and hide.
    4. Tell the dusk story: mice wake when the house goes quiet, which is why we nearly always see only their dash and their tail.
    5. Set the rule with care: if a real mouse ever runs past, our feet stay planted and our voice finds a grown-up — mice are shy, and shy means we let them be.

    Look closer at the picture

    Say mouse and make yourselves tiny — crouched small on the rug, hands up as paws. Ask where the whiskers are on the card, then squeak once, quietly, like a mouse that does not want to be found.

    Ask your child

    "Is the mouse big or tiny?" "What sound does a mouse make?" "Can you tiptoe like a mouse?" "If a real mouse runs by, do we chase it or stay still?" — answered with a squeak, a tiptoe and a firm little pause.

    What your child can say or do

    "Squeak squeak!" Expect tiptoe missions to the kitchen, mice declared behind every cupboard, and sudden whisper-voice games. "Mouse!" may be announced at shadows — smile and agree to investigate slowly.

    Out in the real world

    Mice live near people everywhere — sheds, gardens, park corners at dusk. Real sightings are dashes; that is the whole show, and a fine one: point, gasp quietly, stay planted, tell the grown-up.

    Try it together

    Mouse house: drape a blanket over a chair as the hideout, tiptoe out to collect one block at a time, and stock the larder. A mouse that gathers is a mouse that practises quiet carrying, too.

    Understanding check

    Play a random tiptoe dare tomorrow — "mouse-walk to the door": silent feet and a whispered squeak mean the lesson moved in for good.

    Parent tips

    Keep the squeak indoors and the whisper outdoors; the game doubles as your secret weapon for quiet transitions. If a real mouse appears indoors, stay calm and matter-of-fact — your toddler is reading your face first.

    Staying safe

    A startled wild mouse can nip, so the never-touch rule is absolute — and never follow one into a corner or cupboard. If mice move into the house, that is a grown-up job; cleaning up after them is not for little hands.

    This lesson pairs with the Mouse flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Garden Friends (School Garden).

    LEARNING PATH LESSON · GARDEN FRIENDS · AGES 2 YEARS

    Mole — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    This lesson goes underground: your toddler digs, tunnels and crawls while learning that some garden neighbours spend their whole lives down below, and that is worth a whisper of wonder.

    What is this?

    A mole is a small animal with soft dark fur and big digging paws that lives almost its whole life in tunnels underground. It eats worms and bugs and rarely comes up to the surface.

    What does it mean?

    The mole stretches a toddler’s world downward — there is a whole hidden layer under the lawn. Knowing a creature exists that you hardly ever see is an early lesson in how big the world really is.

    What does the child need to know?

    Moles dig tunnels with strong paws and live in the dark. Meeting one above ground is rare and special — if it ever happens, we whisper, we watch for a moment, and we let it dig on.

    Why this matters

    Digging is deep sensory play — resistance, texture, mess — and tunnelling through blankets builds body awareness in tight spaces. Both are the kind of input busy toddler nervous systems are hungry for.

    What it teaches

    Hand and arm strength (digging, scooping, patting), spatial play (under, through, tunnel), sensory tolerance for the dark and cosy, and the abstract leap of imagining life underground.

    Words to learn

    moledigtunnelundergroundpawsdark

    Say this to your child

    “"A mole! It digs, digs, digs under the garden — tunnels everywhere, all in the dark. Moles have big strong paws for digging. Can you dig a tunnel like the mole does? Can you crawl through it? If we ever see a real one, we whisper — it hardly ever comes up to visit."”

    Step by step

    1. Show the card, say mole, and hold your hands up as digging paws — curl your fingers and show the scooping motion.
    2. Fill a pot with clean soil or head for the sandpit and dig with spoons and cups, narrating the tunnel as it grows longer.
    3. Build a blanket tunnel between two chairs and crawl through it, moles in the dark — a small torch adds real magic.
    4. Tell the truth simply: moles live down there all the time, and their eyes are tiny because the dark is their daytime.
    5. End with the molehill fact: those little soil volcanoes on lawns are mole work — a sign your underground neighbour is busy.

    Look closer at the picture

    Say mole and hold up curled digging paws. Ask where the mole lives — down below, in the dark — then scoop the air twice together. The card shows the tunneller; your hands show the job.

    Ask your child

    "Where does the mole live — up high or down low?" "Can you dig deep like the garden mole?" "Is it light or dark in the tunnel?" "What are those little molehills on the grass?" — answered with digging, crawling and a solemn "down low".

    What your child can say or do

    "Dig dig!" Expect sandpit tunnelling marathons, blanket forts claimed as burrows, and molehills pointed out on every lawn walk. Dark-cosy play may become a bedtime favourite — moles sleep well.

    Out in the real world

    Moles stay hidden but their molehills advertise them on lawns, parks and verges everywhere. Spotting the hill and knowing who built it is your toddler’s first piece of detective natural history.

    Try it together

    Tunnel run: chair-blanket tunnel, crawl through, pat the "soil" (a duvet) flat behind you, then dig a spoon-pot mine in the sandpit and connect the two stories — the same mole, two playrooms.

    Understanding check

    Ask what a mole does all day: "digging!" — with paws demonstrated — means the card moved in. Bonus if the answer arrives from inside a blanket tunnel.

    Parent tips

    Keep digging tools toddler-sized and the soil clean and chemical-free; a dedicated dirt pot beats the flowerbed for repeat play. Join the crawl — tunnels are twice as funny when the tunnel-leader fits badly.

    Staying safe

    Dig in sand, topsoil or a clean plant pot — never where chemicals, pets or unknown muck might be, and no soil in mouths, ever. Blanket tunnels stay low and open-ended so a crawl is always an easy exit; wash hands after all digging.

    This lesson pairs with the Mole flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Garden Friends (School Garden).

    LEARNING PATH LESSON · GARDEN FRIENDS · AGES 2 YEARS

    Lizard — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    This lesson steals the lizard’s daily routine — warm up, stay still, dash — and turns it into a game your toddler can play on any mat, patio or patch of sunshine.

    What is this?

    A lizard is a small reptile with scaly skin, four quick legs and a long tail. It lies flat in sunny spots to warm up, then zips away at the first twitch of danger.

    What does it mean?

    Lizards are the garden’s stillness champions, and stillness is a superpower a two-year-old can actually train. The dash afterwards makes the whole cycle irresistible: wait... wait... GO.

    What does the child need to know?

    Lizards sunbathe on warm rocks and paths to wake their bodies up, and they zoom off when startled. We watch from a step away; grabbing is how lizards lose their tails, and hands stay in pockets near them.

    Why this matters

    Freeze-and-release play is impulse control with a joy at the end — the exact shape of self-regulation your toddler will use at preschool doors for years. And the tail fact lands the no-grabbing rule with a reason that sticks.

    What it teaches

    Stillness on purpose (a milestone at two), listening and responding to the "go" cue, warm-cool and sun-shade vocabulary, body imitation of a totally different body plan, and gentle curiosity about reptiles.

    Words to learn

    lizardsunstillzoomrocktail

    Say this to your child

    “"A lizard! It lies in the sun and gets warm — sss, so still. Can you be a lizard? Lie flat... be still... and when I say fly — ZOOM! Lizards are quick and shy. We watch them from a step away and our hands stay in our pockets, so their tails stay on."”

    Step by step

    1. Show the card, say lizard, and lie down flat on the rug with your arms alongside your body — a sunbathing lizard is a funny sight and an easy copy.
    2. Hold the still together for a slow five-count, whispering warm... warm... warm, then shout fly! and scuttle across the room at full toddler speed.
    3. Play the cycle three times — sunbathe, freeze, zoom — so the order becomes the game and your toddler starts predicting the zoom.
    4. Tell the tail story with feeling: if someone grabs a lizard, the lizard leaves its tail behind and runs — which is why our hands stay tucked.
    5. Finish with a sunny-rock rest: lie flat on a mat by a real window and warm up quietly, lizards together, before the next zoom.

    Look closer at the picture

    Say lizard and lie down flat, arms tucked in, a sunbathing lizard on the rug. Hold still for a slow three-count, ask what the lizard is doing on its rock, then spring up and zoom once around.

    Ask your child

    "What is the lizard doing on the rock?" "Can you be still, still, still?" "What does the lizard do when you say fly?" "Do we touch the lizard, or watch it zoom?" — answered with stillness, a dash and pockets firmly filled.

    What your child can say or do

    "Zoom!" Expect flat-on-the-floor sunbathing in odd corners, freeze-games demanded in queues and shops, and lizards spotted on every warm wall. The still-then-dash rhythm will become a family classic.

    Out in the real world

    Lizards bask on sunny rocks, walls and patios in warm places — and every glimpse is a fast, thrilling rerun. Even without a live one, warm pavements and sunny windowsills keep the story going.

    Try it together

    Lizard rock: designate a cushion as the sunny rock. Lizards must reach it, lie flat, and hold still until you whisper fly — then one lap of the room. Simple, repeatable, and it empties wiggles fast.

    Understanding check

    Call "be a lizard" at a random moment: instant flat stillness followed by an explosive zoom means the lesson is fully installed — warm up, wait, go.

    Parent tips

    Count the stillness out loud and celebrate every extra second — the growing freeze is the progress chart. Keep the zoom zone clear of furniture corners; speed plus joy needs runway.

    Staying safe

    Stillness play happens on rugs and grass, never on roads or driveways. Real lizards are for eyes only — their tails drop when grabbed and wild reptiles can carry salmonella, so hands stay away and get washed after garden play.

    This lesson pairs with the Lizard flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Garden Friends (School Garden).

    LEARNING PATH LESSON · GARDEN FRIENDS · AGES 2 YEARS

    Toad — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    This lesson gives the toad its due: not every pond animal leaps. Your toddler learns the toad walk — low, heavy, slow — and the comparison game that sharpens both animal words at once.

    What is this?

    A toad is a pond animal with dry, bumpy skin and shorter legs than a frog. Instead of jumping high, toads walk and take small hops, and they like gardens as much as ponds.

    What does it mean?

    The toad teaches contrast: same family, different body, different move. For a toddler, spotting how two almost-the-same things differ is a genuine thinking skill — and toad versus frog is the friendliest place to start.

    What does the child need to know?

    Toads walk low and slow on bumpy legs; frogs leap long on springy ones. Both live near water and both stay unhandled — toad skin is bumpy for a reason, and our hands stay off.

    Why this matters

    Comparing two similar things is the toddler version of scientific thinking: notice, compare, name the difference. It also deepens the watching rule — learned twice, on two cards, it sticks twice as well.

    What it teaches

    Comparison and sorting skills, two new movement patterns (walk-low versus leap-long), descriptive vocabulary (bumpy, warty, slow, low), and the widening idea that garden animals come in related pairs.

    Words to learn

    toadwartywalklowhopcompare

    Say this to your child

    “"A toad! Its skin is bumpy — bumpy, bumpy! — and it walks low and slow, not hop-hop like the frog. Can you walk like a toad? Crouch low... heavy steps... good. Toads and frogs both live near the water, and both are look-at friends — hands behind our backs."”

    Step by step

    1. Show the card, say toad, and crouch down low with heavy feet — a toad walk starts with the whole body dropped closer to the floor.
    2. Toad-walk across the rug: slow, low steps with little hops every few paces — different from the frog, and your knees will prove it.
    3. Lay the frog card beside the toad card and compare out loud: this one walks, that one jumps; this skin is bumpy, that one smooth.
    4. Act both animals back to back — leap like the frog, then drop low and walk like the toad — until your toddler switches on your call.
    5. Close the lesson with the shared rule: frogs and toads are both pond friends we watch only, and toads get extra space for their warty skin.

    Look closer at the picture

    Say toad and crouch low with heavy feet. Ask whether this one hops high like the frog or walks low — the bumpy walker — then take two slow toad steps across the rug to settle the argument.

    Ask your child

    "Does the toad jump high or walk low?" "Which one has bumpy skin — toad or frog?" "Can you show me the toad walk?" "Where do toads like to live?" — answered with a crouch, a comparison and a point at the pond side of the room.

    What your child can say or do

    "Toad walk!" Expect dramatic crouch-walking, spontaneous card-pairing on the rug, and toads declared on every damp evening stroll. Frog versus toad may become your toddler’s first debate topic.

    Out in the real world

    Toads turn up in gardens on damp evenings, under pots and logs, walking — always walking — somewhere. Each slow encounter is a rerun of the low walk and the hands-off rule in one go.

    Try it together

    Frog or toad? Call out one and your toddler does the move — high leaps or low walking. Swap roles so your toddler gets to be the caller; naming while directing cements both words.

    Understanding check

    Line up both cards tomorrow and ask which one walks: a toad-shaped crouch is the answer you want — the difference has become your toddler’s own knowledge.

    Parent tips

    Keep the two cards near each other at home; pairs teach better than singletons. If you meet a real toad, admire its warts from a crouch and move along — the comparison game was always the destination.

    Staying safe

    Toad skin can irritate little hands, which makes look-only doubly right — no touching, no licking, no garden kisses, however funny the idea sounds. Wash hands after damp-garden play as standard.

    This lesson pairs with the Toad flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Garden Friends (School Garden).

    LEARNING PATH LESSON · GARDEN FRIENDS · AGES 2 YEARS

    Chipmunk — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    This lesson uses the chipmunk’s best trick — cheeks crammed with food — as a game your toddler can win: gather fast, stash it away, and remember exactly where everything went.

    What is this?

    A chipmunk is a small striped animal, like a squirrel wearing racing stripes down its back. It stuffs seeds into its stretchy cheek pouches and carries them home to its burrow.

    What does it mean?

    The chipmunk is the gather-and-hide specialist, and gathering is a game toddlers are brilliant at. It is also the rare animal lesson that ends with the playroom tidier than it started.

    What does the child need to know?

    Chipmunks carry food in their cheeks and hide it in burrows — and they remember every hiding spot. Wild and quick, they are a watch-only animal, even when the cheeks look funny.

    Why this matters

    Gathering games build working memory (where does it go?), categorising (all the blocks here) and speed with control. And the stash-remembering trick is your toddler’s first memory challenge with a real payoff.

    What it teaches

    Carrying and stashing (whole-arm coordination), memory for hidden places, sorting by kind, fast-but-careful movement, and vocabulary for stripes, cheeks and burrows.

    Words to learn

    chipmunkcheeksstripesgatherburrowseeds

    Say this to your child

    “"A chipmunk! See the stripes — a squirrel with racing stripes! It stuffs food in its big cheeks and carries it to its burrow, and it never forgets where it put things. Can you puff your cheeks? Can you gather like a chipmunk? We watch the little striped friend from far away."”

    Step by step

    1. Show the card, say chipmunk, and puff your own cheeks out big — hold a breath in each one — the picture and the puffed face land together.
    2. Point out the stripes: a chipmunk is a squirrel with racing stripes — then scurry once across the room to prove the speed.
    3. Set up the gather: scatter blocks or toy food on one side of the room, place a basket burrow on the other, and let your chipmunk ferry everything home, cheeks puffed.
    4. Hide one item under a cushion mid-game and ask where it went — chipmunks always remember their stash, and so will your toddler.
    5. Finish with the rule, cheeks still puffed: chipmunks are quick and wild, so we watch them scurry and keep our hands cheerful at our sides.

    Look closer at the picture

    Say chipmunk and puff both cheeks out wide. Ask your toddler to find the stripes running down its back, then scurry to the toy basket and back — one quick chipmunk run, cheeks held the whole way.

    Ask your child

    "What does the chipmunk carry in its cheeks?" "Where does it hide its food?" "Can you scurry like a chipmunk?" "Do we hold the chipmunk, or watch it?" — answered with puffed cheeks, a dash to the basket and a happy head-shake.

    What your child can say or do

    "Cheeks!" Expect puffed-cheek faces at every meal, toys ferried to baskets in chipmunk style, and a suspicious talent for remembering where things were hidden. Tidying-up may never be the same again.

    Out in the real world

    Chipmunks live in woods, parks and gardens in many places, dashing between cover with cheekfuls. Every stripe-and-dash sighting reruns the lesson — point, puff, whisper, admire from the path.

    Try it together

    Cheek pouch relay: your toddler carries one item at a time pressed to their puffed cheeks from pile to burrow — one trip, one item, puff held the whole way. Silly, physical and weirdly calming.

    Understanding check

    Ask tonight where the chipmunk keeps its food: "in its cheeks!" followed by a stash report of hidden toys means the word, the habit and the memory game all landed.

    Parent tips

    Turn the daily tidy into the gather game — chipmunks tidy the burrow, and the burrow is the playroom. Keep the stash-hiding simple: one item, one cushion, one triumphant discovery.

    Staying safe

    Wild chipmunks are quick, jittery and unholdable — hands stay down and snack-feeding is a no, for their diet and yours. If gathering real seeds or nuts outdoors, they go in the basket, not the mouth.

    This lesson pairs with the Chipmunk flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Garden Friends (School Garden).

    LEARNING PATH LESSON · GARDEN FRIENDS · AGES 2 YEARS

    Raccoon — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    This lesson borrows the raccoon’s famous habit — dunking and rubbing everything in water — and turns it into washing play your toddler can own, with the mask as the memory hook.

    What is this?

    A raccoon is a medium-sized animal with grey fur, a striped tail and a black mask of fur around its eyes. It has clever little hands and gives its snacks a famous wash in water before eating.

    What does it mean?

    The raccoon gives your toddler two gifts: an unmistakable picture to name (the mask!) and a washing habit worth copying. Clever hands, it turns out, wash their food — and little hands can too.

    What does the child need to know?

    Raccoons wear a black mask, work at night, and dunk their snacks in water to give them a good rub. They are wild night visitors — clever hands or not, we never try to hold one.

    Why this matters

    The wash-your-food story is a Trojan horse for hand-washing pride: if a raccoon washes everything, so can we. And the mask makes this the easiest animal on the whole set for a toddler to spot and name from a book.

    What it teaches

    Fine motor in water (rubbing, scrubbing, patting), the mask-as-identity idea (great for face vocabulary), night-and-day sorting, and hygiene habits smuggled in as animal play.

    Words to learn

    raccoonmasknightwashpawsclever

    Say this to your child

    “"A raccoon! See the black mask painted on its face — a little bandit! Raccoons have clever hands and they wash their food in water, rub-a-dub. Can you wash your toy like a raccoon? Raccoons come out at night. If one visits the garden, we watch from the window — clever hands stay wild."”

    Step by step

    1. Show the card, say raccoon, and draw an imaginary mask around your own eyes with two fingers — the mask is the word’s best friend.
    2. Rub your hands together like a raccoon giving its food a wash — quick little scrubbing motions, and wait for the copy.
    3. Set a washing station: a shallow bowl of water, a few washable toys, and a towel — dunk, rub, pat, line up the clean ones like the raccoon would.
    4. Tell the night story: raccoons wake up when we go to bed, which is why the bin sometimes looks surprised in the morning.
    5. Land the rule kindly: raccoons are clever wild animals, so we watch them from windows and never reach out — wild hands and toddler hands do not mix.

    Look closer at the picture

    Say raccoon and draw a pretend mask around your eyes with two fingers. Ask what is black on the raccoon’s face, then rub your palms together like clever paws giving a toy its wash.

    Ask your child

    "What is black around the raccoon’s eyes?" "What does the raccoon do with its food?" "When is the raccoon awake — day or night?" "Do we touch the raccoon, or watch from far away?" — answered with mask-fingers, a scrub and a whisper.

    What your child can say or do

    "Mask!" Expect finger-masks around eyes at random, toy-washing stations appearing at every puddle, and raccoons blamed for midnight noises. Hand-washing may gain a raccoon soundtrack — take the win.

    Out in the real world

    Raccoons prowl gardens, parks and bins after dark in many places; most toddler sightings are from windows, which is exactly right. Each masked face in a book reruns the lesson instantly.

    Try it together

    Raccoon wash day: line up three toys, dunk and rub each one in the bowl, dry them, and repeat until the water is much too busy. Add a washcloth for the table afterwards — the raccoon cleans up, too.

    Understanding check

    Watch tonight’s hand-wash: if the rubbing comes with raccoon narrations, the habit and the animal are bonded — the lesson is complete and the sink is a Pond now.

    Parent tips

    Keep the washing bowl shallow and on a towel; raccoon play is wet play, and wet play needs a floor plan. Extend the mask idea to other faces — pandas, badgers — and watch the spotting skill generalise.

    Staying safe

    Raccoons can carry diseases and bite when cornered — window-watching is the whole friendship, and bin visits are grown-up business. After water play, empty the bowl and dry the floor so nobody skates.

    This lesson pairs with the Raccoon flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Garden Friends (School Garden).

    LEARNING PATH LESSON · GARDEN FRIENDS · AGES 2 YEARS

    Deer — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    This lesson brings the quiet bigness of the deer indoors: slow tiptoes, listening ears and a first understanding that the biggest garden neighbours need the biggest distance.

    What is this?

    A deer is a large, gentle animal with long legs, big ears and soft fur that lives in woods and fields. Deer hear everything and move away fast and quietly.

    What does it mean?

    The deer stretches a toddler’s sense of scale — this neighbour is taller than you and still shy. Meeting bigness that needs space (not hugging) is an early lesson in how wild things stay well.

    What does the child need to know?

    Deer have big listening ears and long quiet legs. They are large wild animals: gentle to look at, never to approach. We watch from far away — through a window or from the path — and we speak in whispers.

    Why this matters

    Distance is a hard idea for toddlers, who show love by reaching. The deer card gives distance a positive shape: the farther away you are, the longer the deer stays — watching becomes a game of patience with a giant prize.

    What it teaches

    Whisper-level quiet, listening attention (what did we hear?), scale words (big, tall, huge), self-restraint with a visible reward, and the idea that size and wildness travel together.

    Words to learn

    deertallearsquietwoodsfar

    Say this to your child

    “"A deer! So tall, so quiet. Deer have big ears that turn and listen — can you make deer ears? They live in the woods and they move away softly. When we see a deer, we stay far away and whisper — that is how we say we love you to a deer."”

    Step by step

    1. Show the card, say deer, and hold a hand high above your head — bigger than you, bigger than me — so the size arrives before the details.
    2. Make deer ears with your hands and swivel them slowly: deer listen all the time, and so will we for this game.
    3. Tiptoe across the room, freeze at every creak, and listen — the deer walk is tiptoe plus stop plus listen, repeated.
    4. Explain the distance rule in toddler terms: deer stay happy when we stay far; if we tiptoe closer, they vanish — so the game is to be the stillness they trust.
    5. End by looking out of a window or across a field together and counting what a deer might hear from there — a bird, a car, your whisper.

    Look closer at the picture

    Say deer and hold a hand high — taller than you, taller than me. Make swivelling ear-hands together, ask what the deer is doing on the card, then drop to a whisper: deer talk is quiet talk.

    Ask your child

    "Is the deer big or little?" "What are its ears doing?" "Show me the deer tiptoe." "Do we walk close to the deer, or stay far away?" — answered with ear-hands, a tiptoe and a stretched-out "faaar".

    What your child can say or do

    "Deer! Big one!" Expect ear-hands at bedtime, deer declared at the far end of parks, and sudden freezing mid-walk — ears up, listening. The whisper may spread to libraries and churches, courtesy of the deer.

    Out in the real world

    Deer appear at forest edges, parklands and safari-park windows, often at dawn or dusk. Each tall, quiet sighting is a rerun: freeze, whisper, count the seconds it stays — distance paying its dividend.

    Try it together

    Listening walk: indoors or out, tiptoe together and stop every few steps to name one sound you can both hear. Deer ears swivelling, toddler listening — attention training with antler-level dignity.

    Understanding check

    At the next deer-in-a-book moment, watch the volume: if your toddler drops to a whisper and stays planted, the distance rule has become instinct — the lesson is complete.

    Parent tips

    Let the deer own the vocabulary of quiet: "deer feet" for tiptoeing past a sleeping baby is a household trick with a long shelf life. If a safari park is ever nearby, the window view is the field trip.

    Staying safe

    Deer are large wild animals — never approach, feed or chase one, however calm it looks; a startled deer is powerful and unpredictable. Keep toddlers inside fences and in hands at safari parks and forest edges.

    This lesson pairs with the Deer flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Garden Friends (School Garden).

    LEARNING PATH LESSON · GARDEN FRIENDS · AGES 2 YEARS

    Snake — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    This lesson handles the garden’s most serious card with a calm voice and a playful prop: scarf snakes to wiggle and coil, plus the honest rule delivered without drama or fear.

    What is this?

    A snake is a long animal with no legs that slithers smoothly over the ground. Garden snakes lie in sunny spots to warm up and mostly want to be left alone.

    What does it mean?

    The snake card is where the garden set gets serious, and toddlers can feel the shift. Handled calmly, it teaches the deepest safety lesson of all: some rules exist because the world has real edges.

    What does the child need to know?

    Snakes slither and like the sun. The rule comes in three moves: we never touch a snake, we step back slowly, and we tell a grown-up right away. Snakes are not nasty — they simply want their space, and we give it.

    Why this matters

    A two-year-old who can name the rule and the move owns it. Fear is not the goal — respect is. Calm repetition of a clear rule beats alarm, and the scarf game keeps the snake friendly in imagination while the rule stays real.

    What it teaches

    Rule-learning with three clear steps, calm body response (step back, not scream), long-and-short vocabulary, scarf play for arm strength and coordination, and trust that grown-ups handle the scary bits.

    Words to learn

    snakeslithersunlongbacktell

    Say this to your child

    “"A snake — sssss. It is long and it slithers on its belly, with no legs at all. Here is our snake rule, and it is an important one: we never touch snakes. If we ever see one, we step back slowly and we tell me. A snake’s whole wish is to be left in peace — and peace is what we give it."”

    Step by step

    1. Show the card, say snake, and make a long sssss — long and slow, the sound the animal makes in every storybook.
    2. Draw the shape with your arm: a snake is one long curve with no legs — let your toddler trace it in the air with a finger.
    3. Grab a long scarf — your stand-in snake — and wriggle it over the floor together, then coil it in a warm circle for its nap.
    4. Say the rule in three beats, keeping your voice level and kind: see a snake — step back slowly — tell a grown-up. Practise the three beats like a little song.
    5. Close with calm: snakes live in the garden too, and they are happiest when we give them room — the scarf snake can live in the toy box, the real one stays outside.

    Look closer at the picture

    Say snake and stretch one arm into a long, slow curve — no legs anywhere. Make the sssss sound softly, ask what the snake is doing in the sun, and trace its long shape on the rug with one finger.

    Ask your child

    "What does the snake say?" "How many legs does a snake have?" "What do we do if we see a real snake?" "Who do we tell?" — the last two answered with the practised chant: step back, tell you.

    What your child can say or do

    "Sssss!" "Step back, tell Mummy!" Expect scarf snakes everywhere, snakes audited in every picture book, and the rule recited with solemn pride. Calm respect — not fear — is the sound of this lesson working.

    Out in the real world

    Garden snakes sun themselves on warm paths, walls and woodpiles in many places. Every real sighting — rare and brief — is the rule performed exactly as rehearsed: back slowly, find the grown-up.

    Try it together

    Scarf snake trail: lay the scarf in wiggles along the floor and walk the line heel-to-toe like a tightrope, then coil it in a basket for its nap. Wiggles out, rule intact, snake tucked in.

    Understanding check

    Ask casually what we do if we find a snake outside: the three-beat answer — back slowly, tell a grown-up, never touch — means the most important rule in the set is home.

    Parent tips

    Keep your voice flat and warm when the rule comes up; drama teaches fear where calm teaches competence. Retell the rule in new places — parks, holidays, grandma’s garden — so it travels like the scarf does.

    Staying safe

    This is the set’s real-deal safety card: never touch, reach for or corner any snake, and treat every unknown snake as a keep-away snake. If one appears often near your home, mention it to local wildlife services — not to your toddler.

    This lesson pairs with the Snake flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Garden Friends (School Garden).

    LEARNING PATH LESSON · GARDEN FRIENDS · AGES 2 YEARS

    Bat — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    This lesson turns the day on its head: while the rest of the garden goes to sleep, the bat wakes up. Your toddler hangs, flaps and peers at dusk for the garden’s night shift.

    What is this?

    A bat is a small furry animal with wings that flies at night. Bats twist and dart after insects in the dark and sleep through the day hanging upside down.

    What does it mean?

    The bat introduces a deliciously strange idea: some neighbours keep opposite hours. Upside-down sleeping and flying by night make the bat the set’s wonder card — the one that says the world is bigger than my bedtime.

    What does the child need to know?

    Bats fly at night and hang upside down to sleep. They are wild animals that are never touched or carried — but watching their fast zigzags over the garden at dusk is a airshow, and it is all ours.

    Why this matters

    Dusk-watching is a wind-down ritual with a thrill in it: the sky empties of birds and fills with bats just as curtains close. A toddler who knows who flies at night watches the evening sky with ownership instead of sleepiness.

    What it teaches

    Body inversion play (bending to hang is a novel vestibular treat), day-night sorting, quiet evening attention, flapping large-movement play, and comfort with the dark — a bat is a friendly face for it.

    Words to learn

    batnightwingshangflydark

    Say this to your child

    “"A bat! Night flyer — flap, flap, flap. When the sun goes down, the bat wakes up and catches bugs in the dark. And guess how it sleeps? Upside down, hanging by its toes! We watch bats from the ground and the window — they are wild flyers, and the sky is theirs."”

    Step by step

    1. Show the card, say bat, and flap your hands like small quick wings — bats flutter, fast and jittery, not slow and soaring.
    2. Do the bat hang: bend forward at the hips, arms dangling down, head low — a bat at rest. Hold it, wobble happily, then rise.
    3. Dim the lights and fly: flap around the room together as night bats hunting — a few laps is plenty; bats tire, and so do knees.
    4. Tell the upside-down fact with wonder: bats sleep with their feet holding on, heads pointing at the ground — every toddler’s favourite nonsense that is true.
    5. End at a window at dusk, if you can: look up, watch for fast flickers, and whisper bat! for each zigzag you spot together.

    Look closer at the picture

    Say bat and flap quick little hand-wings, fast and fluttery. Ask when the bat flies — at night, when we sleep — then bend forward and dangle like a bat at rest, toes holding on, head hanging low.

    Ask your child

    "When does the bat fly — day or night?" "Can you hang like a bat?" "How does a bat sleep?" "Do we touch the bat, or watch the sky?" — answered with a dangle, a gasp of delight and a point at the ceiling.

    What your child can say or do

    "Bat! Night-night up!" Expect upside-down facts recited at dinner, bat-hangs off the sofa arm, and requests to check the sky before bed. The dusk vigil may become a treasured slow-down ritual.

    Out in the real world

    Bats flicker over gardens, parks and street lamps at dusk almost everywhere — a two-minute sky-watch usually finds one. Each zigzag reruns the lesson, and the window is the best seat in the house.

    Try it together

    Moths and bats: you be the slow moth wandering the room, and your bat chases with flapping hands — then swap. A soft "swoosh" sound makes the hunting official.

    Understanding check

    Point at the darkening sky tomorrow evening without a word: if your toddler whispers "bat!" at the first flicker, the card has given your family a nightly wonder — lesson complete.

    Parent tips

    Keep the hanging game to sofas, beds and rugs — heads and floors negotiate poorly. If a real bat ever gets indoors, do not involve small hands: close the door, call for help, and save the story for breakfast.

    Staying safe

    Bats are strictly wild: never touch or pick one up, indoors or out — they can scratch and carry diseases, and only animal-carers should handle them. Dusk-watching happens behind glass or on a held hand, well away from open water and edges.

    This lesson pairs with the Bat flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Garden Friends (School Garden).

    LEARNING PATH LESSON · GARDEN FRIENDS · AGES 2 YEARS

    Owl — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    This lesson is built for the end of the day: wide owl eyes, two soft hoots, lights down low. The garden’s night guard becomes the friendliest possible bridge into sleep.

    What is this?

    An owl is a large night bird with big round eyes, silent wings and sharp talons. It watches and listens for mice in the dark and hoots to talk to other owls.

    What does it mean?

    The owl closes the set with a comforting swap: when your toddler goes to bed, someone else takes the night shift. A garden with a night guard is a garden that is never truly empty — and that is a cozy thought, not a scary one.

    What does the child need to know?

    Owls doze through the daylight and do their hunting after dark, with huge eyes that see in the dark and a hoot that carries. We hoot softly, we look for them in books and windows, and we let them work their quiet shift.

    Why this matters

    Bedtime needs rituals, and the owl lends its whole shape to one: eyes wide, two hoots, lights low. The night-bird idea also reframes darkness — the dark is when the owl is busy, and that makes the dark a workplace, not a monster.

    What it teaches

    Eye and face imitation (the owl stare is a genuine expressive milestone), soft-voice control (hoots only get quieter), day-night mastery, and a bedtime-specific calm that parents will reuse nightly.

    Words to learn

    owlnighteyeshootwingssleep

    Say this to your child

    “"Hoo-hoo! The owl owns the night. Big round eyes, silent wings — it watches the garden while we sleep. Can you make your big owl eyes? Can you hoot softly? Hoo... hoo... When you are in bed, the owl is just starting its day — the garden is in good paws and wings."”

    Step by step

    1. Show the card, say owl, and open your own eyes as wide as they will go — hold the stare, do not blink, and watch your toddler try to match it.
    2. Hoot together, twice and softly — hoo-hoo — cupping your mouth like a little horn; loud hoots are for another day.
    3. Turn your head slowly side to side, owl-style, without moving your shoulders — the slow swivel is irresistible to copy.
    4. Tell the night story in a low voice: when we sleep, the owl opens its big eyes and watches over the garden — quiet wings, soft hoots, all night long.
    5. End the lesson as a ritual: lights down, one wide-eyed look, two whispered hoots at each other — and off to sleep, while the owl takes the watch.

    Look closer at the picture

    Say owl and open your eyes as round as big coins — hold the stare and see who blinks first. Ask where the owl’s big eyes are on the card, then hoot twice, soft as a goodnight. Hoo... hoo...

    Ask your child

    "When is the owl awake?" "What do its eyes look like?" "Can you give me a soft hoot?" "Who watches the garden at night?" — answered with a wide stare, a whisper-hoot and a snug little smile.

    What your child can say or do

    "Hoo-hoo!" Expect wide-eye contests across the dinner table, hoots exchanged over the baby monitor, and owls located in every moonlit illustration. The hoot may become your household’s official goodnight.

    Out in the real world

    Owls hoot from tall trees and rooftops at night in many neighbourhoods; most toddlers meet them in books first, which suits the bedtime angle. A real evening hoot from a window is pure gold — whisper it back.

    Try it together

    Owl eyes contest: sit face to face in the dim light, open eyes wide, and see who blinks first — loser hoots. Calm, silly, and the finest pre-bed wind-down in this whole set.

    Understanding check

    Tonight at lights-out, listen for it: two soft hoots from the cot mean the lesson has become the ritual — the owl now owns the hour before sleep.

    Parent tips

    Reserve this card for the last slot of any session; its power is the descent into quiet. Keep hoots whisper-level and the room dim — the owl works best as a lullaby with feathers.

    Staying safe

    Owls are wild hunters with real talons — admire them from windows, books and sanctuaries only, and never approach a perched or grounded owl. Any owl found on the ground needs a wildlife rescuer, not a rescuing toddler.

    This lesson pairs with the Owl flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Garden Friends (School Garden).
